680.title: Diwali: the row of lamps
680.hook: before dawn in the South, Krishna breaks Naraka's fortress open and the captives walk free
680.carry: god comes down to set the captive free
680.howItsDone: In much of South India, Deepavali is celebrated before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi with an oil bath, new clothes, firecrackers and sweets; in many other regions that day is a smaller lamp-lighting the day before the main Diwali night.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, one Goddess in nine forms. ekam sat: one truth, many names.
screen: `EKAM SAT: ONE TRUTH, MANY NAMES.`

segments.voice: In Tamil Nadu, a family's Deepavali can begin around four in the morning. Someone wakes the house while it's still pitch dark. Each person sits down, and an elder rubs warm sesame oil into their hair. Then a hot bath, new clothes, a firecracker before sunrise, sweets for breakfast. In North India, Diwali is usually a night: the lamps come out after dark, for Rama coming home. Same festival name. Different hour, different story. This one isn't about Rama at all.
screen: `FOUR IN THE MORNING.` → `WARM OIL, A HOT BATH, NEW CLOTHES.` → `A DIFFERENT STORY.`

segments.voice: The story belongs to Krishna and a demon king named Naraka, and the Bhagavata Purana tells it. Naraka has grown arrogant and cruel. He has stolen treasures from the gods, among them the earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and he holds thousands of young women captive in his fortress city. Krishna flies there on Garuda, his wife Satyabhama beside him, breaks through the fortress walls, and kills Naraka in battle. Then he opens the fortress. The women held there, sixteen thousand one hundred in the Bhagavata's count, walk out free. In the text they choose him as their husband, and he sends them to Dvaraka and marries them all. Many families add that Naraka, dying, asked for his day to be remembered with lights. That's Naraka Chaturdashi, the day before the main Diwali night, and in much of South India it is Deepavali, kept before dawn. The oil bath, people say, recalls Krishna bathing after the battle. Now the teaching under it. For Hindus, Krishna is Vishnu come down into the world: an avatar, a word that means one who descends. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says why he comes: whenever goodness is failing, age after age, he takes birth to protect the good and set things right. So the lamps aren't only for a win. They're for a God who doesn't stay far off while people are trapped. He comes down, breaks the walls, and opens the door. Rama coming home, the captives walking free: two roads to the same row of lamps.
screen: `NARAKA: A CRUEL KING, A FORTRESS.` · `KRISHNA AND SATYABHAMA ON GARUDA.` · `THE CAPTIVES WALK FREE.` · `AVATAR: THE ONE WHO COMES DOWN.` · then, large: `GOD COMES DOWN TO SET THE CAPTIVE FREE.`

segments.voice: Many families set a small clay lamp, a diya, at the front door on Deepavali. Light one small light, or picture one. Think of someone who is stuck somewhere: a hard job, an illness, a lonely stretch. If you pray, say a name of Krishna or Vishnu and ask for them. If you don't, simply hold them in mind beside the light, at the door of the place they're stuck. You don't have to fix anything. Just keep the lamp at their door.
Diwali. In much of the South, Deepavali comes before dawn on Naraka Chaturdashi, remembering Krishna's victory and the captives set free.
screen: `DIWALI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: god comes down to set the captive free. That's what the lamp at the door remembers. See you tomorrow.

681.title: Holi: the festival of colors
681.hook: little Krishna colors Radha's face; in Braj, Holi is his divine play, and everyone joins in
681.carry: holi is krishna's play, and everyone's invited
681.tomorrow: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
681.howItsDone: In the Braj region around Mathura and Vrindavan, Holi is celebrated over a week or more, with Lathmar Holi in Barsana and Nandgaon, flower Holi in Vrindavan's temples, and songs of Krishna and Radha; elsewhere many families tell both Prahlad's story and Krishna's.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Deepavali before dawn, and Krishna, God come down, breaking Naraka's fortress open. God comes down to set the captive free.
screen: `GOD COMES DOWN TO SET THE CAPTIVE FREE.`

segments.voice: A little boy runs to his mother, upset. Why is Radha so fair, he asks, and I'm so dark? It isn't fair. His mother, smiling, has an idea. Go and color her face, she says, any color you like. Then you'll match. The boy is Krishna, the mother Yashoda, and that small story, told and sung all over the Braj country where Krishna grew up, is one of the reasons people there say Holi began.
screen: `WHY IS SHE FAIR AND I'M DARK?` → `GO AND COLOR HER FACE.` → `KRISHNA'S COLOR.`

segments.voice: Braj is the region around Mathura and Vrindavan, south of Delhi, where Krishna's childhood stories are set. In Braj, Holi isn't one day; it's a season of a week or more. In Barsana, the village tradition remembers as Radha's, there's Lathmar Holi, Holi of the sticks. Men from Nandgaon, Krishna's village, come over to throw color, and the women of Barsana meet them with long sticks, playfully beating them while the men hide under shields and everyone sings. The next day, it happens the other way around in Nandgaon. In Vrindavan's temples, there's a day when priests throw flower petals over the crowd. Many families tell two stories: the fire the night before, for Prahlad, and the colors the next day, which in Braj belong to Krishna. Now the teaching. Hindus have a word for what Krishna does in Braj: lila, divine play. The God who holds the universe steals butter, teases his mother, and throws color. And in Braj devotion, Radha's love for Krishna is the model of bhakti: loving God the way you love the person closest to you, with joy, not fear. That's why Holi there isn't a show to watch. Everyone joins the play, young and old, rich and poor, Barsana and Nandgaon. Under the color, nobody can tell who's who. Many devotees read that as the point: in Krishna's play, the faces are level, and everyone's invited in.
screen: `BRAJ: KRISHNA'S COUNTRY.` · `LATHMAR HOLI: STICKS AND SHIELDS.` · `LILA: GOD AT PLAY.` · `BHAKTI: LOVE, NOT FEAR.` · then, large: `EVERYONE'S INVITED INTO THE PLAY.`

segments.voice: In Vrindavan, people greet each other with two words: Radhe Radhe. Think of someone you feel slightly apart from: a different age, different politics, a different background. Picture both your faces covered in the same bright pink powder, so nobody could say which is which. If you pray, say Radhe Radhe for them, silently. If you don't, just wish them well. Let any small grudge slide off with the color.
Holi. In Braj it's Krishna's lila, his season of play, with sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan, and every face the same bright mess.

682.title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
682.hook: the gods churn the ocean, poison rises first, and Shiva drinks it; why devotees stay up all night
682.carry: nilakantha: god takes the poison so others live
682.tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
682.howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus keep vigil at Shiva temples through the night, chanting and offering water, milk and bilva leaves to the lingam; some connect the night with Shiva drinking the poison from the churned ocean.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi in Braj, Krishna's lila, sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan. Holi is Krishna's play, and everyone's invited.
screen: `HOLI IS KRISHNA'S PLAY, AND EVERYONE'S INVITED.`

segments.voice: Look closely at many images of Shiva, and his throat is a darker blue than the rest of him. It isn't a painting mistake; it's a scar, of a kind. One of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. And one story people tell about Maha Shivaratri is how his throat got that color: a moment when the whole universe nearly ended, and one god drank the danger so everyone else could live.
screen: `A BLUE THROAT.` → `NILAKANTHA.` → `THE NIGHT HE DRANK THE DANGER.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. The gods and the demons, usually enemies, agree to work together for once. They want amrita, the nectar of immortality, at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they churn the ocean, the samudra manthan, with the mountain Mandara as the churning stick and the great serpent Vasuki as the rope, gods pulling one end, demons the other. But the first thing that rises isn't nectar. It's poison: Halahala, so strong its fumes spread in every direction and begin to burn the worlds. Gods, demons, every creature, run to Shiva. The text says Shiva looks on them with compassion, and his wife, the Goddess, agrees. He gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. And in the telling many know, he holds it in his throat, not swallowed, not spat out, and his throat turns blue. That's the teaching in the blue throat. Shiva is Mahadeva, the great god, and here greatness means this: when the poison comes, he's the one who takes it in, so the world can live. Devotees answer him on Shivaratri. Many fast, stay awake through the night, and pour water and milk over the lingam, chanting Om Namah Shivaya. Some say the vigil echoes the churning, when the gods stayed up singing to Shiva while he held the poison; some say the cool water soothes his burning throat. These are explanations people give, among several. But the shape is clear: God held the hard thing for us, and for one night, we stay up with him.
screen: `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `FIRST, NOT NECTAR, BUT POISON.` · `HELD IN THE THROAT: NILAKANTHA.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA, ALL NIGHT.` · then, large: `GOD TAKES THE POISON SO OTHERS LIVE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say Om Namah Shivaya slowly, with your breath, the way devotees chant it through the night. If you don't, simply breathe. Then bring to mind one person you love who's holding something hard right now, something they can't swallow and can't spit out: a worry, a grief. Don't fix it. Keep them company in it for a few breaths, the way devotees keep Shiva company.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, the blue-throated one, who held the world's poison so others could live.
screen: `SHIVARATRI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Nilakantha, god takes the poison so others live. Tomorrow, a thread tied during a losing war. Day six hundred eighty-two, done.

683.title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
683.hook: the gods are losing a war, and Indra's wife ties a thread of protection on his wrist
683.carry: raksha: a prayer of protection, and a promise
683.tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
683.howItsDone: On Shravana Purnima, besides sisters tying rakhis on brothers, many priests tie protective threads on the wrists of the families they serve while reciting a short Sanskrit verse remembering King Bali; in some communities the same day is also when men renew their sacred thread.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shivaratri, and Shiva's blue throat, the poison held so others could live. Nilakantha: god takes the poison so others live.
screen: `GOD TAKES THE POISON SO OTHERS LIVE.`

segments.voice: Before rakhis came with glitter and cartoon characters, a protective thread was serious business. Priests in many parts of India still go house to house on the full moon of Shravana, tying a plain thread on the wrists of the families they serve, with a short Sanskrit verse. The verse mentions a demon king. And behind the custom, the Puranas tell of a war the gods were losing, and a wife who tied the thread.
screen: `A PRIEST AT THE DOOR.` → `A PLAIN THREAD, A SHORT VERSE.` → `A WAR THE GODS WERE LOSING.`

segments.voice: The story is told in the Bhavishya Purana. Indra, king of the gods, has been fighting the demons a long time, and he's losing, worn out and afraid. His wife, Shachi, also called Indrani, goes to the gods' teacher, Brihaspati, for help. He tells her: on the full moon of Shravana, prepare a raksha, a protective thread, with the proper rites, and tie it on Indra's wrist. She does. Indra goes back into battle with the thread on his arm, and this time he wins. Notice who ties it: a wife, not a sister. Now, the priests' verse. It remembers the demon king Bali, who was bound by Vishnu. Its sense: with the thread that bound the mighty Bali, king of the demons, I bind you; stay firm, O protection, stay firm. So the verse asks the thread to hold the person the way Bali was held. Here's the teaching in the knot. A raksha isn't jewelry; it's a prayer you can wear, tied on with a sacred verse. In Shachi's story, it guards the one who wears it. In the custom families keep today, the one who wears it also takes something on: a duty to look after the one who tied it. Hindus call a duty like that dharma. So a rakhi carries two things at once, a blessing given and a promise accepted, and it can be tied by a wife, a priest, a sister, a cousin or a friend.
screen: `INDRA IS LOSING THE WAR.` · `SHACHI TIES THE THREAD.` · `THE VERSE: AS BALI WAS BOUND.` · `A PRAYER YOU CAN WEAR.` · then, large: `A BLESSING GIVEN, A PROMISE ACCEPTED.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus wear a red or yellow thread tied at a puja for days afterward. If you have a thread, tie it on your wrist now; if not, picture one. Think of someone who protected you without making a fuss: a parent who waited up, a friend who stood beside you. If you pray, say their name and ask God to protect them. If you don't, simply thank them in your mind. Then think of one person you'd protect, and let the thread be your promise to them.
Rakhi. A thread of protection, tied in the old story by Shachi on Indra's wrist, and today by sisters, cousins, priests and friends: a blessing and a promise.
screen: `RAKHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: raksha, a prayer of protection, and a promise. Tomorrow, a baby nobody could hold. See you then.

684.title: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born
684.hook: a baby girl carried back to Kamsa's prison slips from his hands and rises as the Goddess
684.carry: yogamaya: no tyrant can hold god's power
684.howItsDone: Many Hindus fast on Janmashtami until midnight, the hour of Krishna's birth, then sing, rock a small cradle with an image of baby Krishna, and break the fast; many keep the next day as Nandotsava, and in many places Yogamaya is honored as the Goddess who protected the infant Krishna.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakhi, and the thread Shachi tied on Indra's wrist. Raksha: a prayer of protection, and a promise.
screen: `A PRAYER OF PROTECTION, AND A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Krishna's birth is usually told as the story of one baby: the boy carried across the flooded river. But Vasudeva didn't come back from Gokul empty-handed. He laid his son beside the sleeping Yashoda and picked up her newborn daughter, then walked back through the storm to the prison, and the doors locked behind him. In the morning, Kamsa would come for the eighth child. And the eighth child, now, was a girl.
screen: `THE BABY CARRIED BACK.` → `YASHODA'S DAUGHTER.` → `KAMSA COMES IN THE MORNING.`

segments.voice: The baby cries, and the guards run to tell the king. Kamsa rushes in. Devaki begs him: you've killed my sons; this is a daughter, she can't hurt you, let me keep just this one. He doesn't listen. In the Bhagavata's telling, he grabs the baby by the feet to dash her against a stone, and she slips out of his hands. She rises into the air, no longer a newborn: the Goddess, eight-armed, holding weapons, shining. The text calls her Yogamaya, Vishnu's own power, who had agreed to be born to Yashoda for exactly this night. From the sky she tells Kamsa: killing me does you no good. The one who will end you has already been born, somewhere else. Then she's gone. And the Bhagavata does something surprising. Kamsa, shaken, apologizes to Devaki and Vasudeva and frees them from their chains. It doesn't last; by the next day his advisers have talked him back into cruelty. Here's the teaching folded into the night. Kamsa has the prison, the guards, the chains and the stone, and none of it can hold God's power. That's what Yogamaya shows him. The God who came down was born in a prison, and the darkest room in the kingdom couldn't keep him. So on Janmashtami many families fast until midnight, then sing and rock a small cradle for baby Krishna, welcoming the one no tyrant could hold.

685.title: Ganesh Chaturthi: welcoming Ganesha home
685.hook: Ganesha eats Kubera's whole feast and stays hungry, until one handful given with love fills him
685.carry: ganesha counts the love, not the feast
685.howItsDone: On the last day of Ganesh Chaturthi, often Anant Chaturdashi, families perform a final aarti, offer food for the journey, ask forgiveness for any lapse as hosts, and carry the image to water, chanting Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Janmashtami, and the baby girl who rose from Kamsa's hands. Yogamaya: no tyrant can hold god's power.
screen: `NO TYRANT CAN HOLD GOD'S POWER.`

segments.voice: A story told in many homes at Ganesh Chaturthi. Kubera, the god of wealth, wants everyone to see how rich he is, so he invites Shiva to a feast. Shiva sends his son instead: Ganesha, small and round. Kubera serves him course after course, and Ganesha eats it all. Then the rest of the kitchen. Then, the story says, the furniture, and he's still hungry. Kubera runs to Shiva in a panic. And the boy's parents give him one small handful of food, offered with love. Ganesha eats it, and he's full.
screen: `KUBERA'S FEAST.` → `GANESHA EATS EVERYTHING.` → `ONE HANDFUL, GIVEN WITH LOVE.`

segments.voice: That story is the key to Ganesh Chaturthi, a festival kept for a day and a half, or five, seven or ten days. Families invite Ganesha in as a guest of honor and feed him modaks, sweets, fruit, flowers. Not because God needs a meal; Kubera's whole palace couldn't fill him. What fills him is bhava, the love behind the offering. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says the same: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, offered with love, I accept. It's one of the plainest teachings in Hinduism: God counts the love, not the size of the plate. Then comes the last day, Anant Chaturdashi. Before the image leaves home, the family gathers for a final aarti, offers food for the road, often curd rice or modaks, and asks forgiveness for anything they did wrong as hosts. At the water, the crowd shouts one call, in Marathi: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Ganpati, our dear father, Morya: next year, come early. Bappa is an affectionate word, like dad. Morya is often linked to Morya Gosavi, a Ganesha saint remembered at Chinchwad near Pune. Then the image is carried in and slowly let go: visarjan, a word whose root sense is closer to releasing. People cry, grown men too. But the guest has been loved, fed and thanked, and the last word isn't goodbye. It's come back soon.
screen: `NOT THE FEAST: THE LOVE.` · `BHAVA: THE LOVE BEHIND THE OFFERING.` · `FOOD FOR THE ROAD, AND FORGIVENESS.` · `GANPATI BAPPA MORYA!` · then, large: `GANESHA COUNTS THE LOVE, NOT THE FEAST.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus offer food to God before they eat it, then receive it back as prasad. Take one small thing: a sip of water, a flower, a piece of fruit. If you pray, hold it up for Ganesha, or for God as you know God, and offer it with your whole heart. If you don't pray, offer it in your mind to someone you love, and mean it. Then, on an out-breath, say what the crowd says: come back soon.
Ganesh Chaturthi. Up to ten days of feeding a guest who is filled by love, ending with visarjan and the cry Ganpati Bappa Morya: come back soon.

686.title: Vijayadashami: Rama's lotus for Durga
686.hook: before fighting Ravana, Rama offers Durga 108 lotuses, and one is missing
686.carry: shakti: even rama bowed to the goddess first
686.tomorrow: Bali Pratipada: the demon king welcomed home
686.howItsDone: Navaratri ends on Vijayadashami: many North Indian towns stage the Ramlila and burn Ravana's effigy on Dussehra; in Bengal, Durga's image is immersed after sindoor khela; in much of the South, families honor tools and books on Ayudha Puja, the ninth day, and on the tenth many children begin learning to write.

screen: `DAY SIX-HUNDRED-EIGHTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ganesha's farewell, and Kubera's feast that couldn't fill him. Ganesha counts the love, not the feast.
screen: `GANESHA COUNTS THE LOVE, NOT THE FEAST.`

segments.voice: On the same autumn day, in three corners of India, three different things are happening. In a Delhi park, a crowd watches a giant paper-and-bamboo Ravana as someone fires a flaming arrow into it. In Kolkata, married women smear red sindoor on each other's faces, laughing and crying, before an image of Durga about to leave for the river. In a Kerala home, a small child writes their first letters in a plate of rice. It's all one day: the tenth.
screen: `A BURNING RAVANA IN DELHI.` → `RED SINDOOR IN KOLKATA.` → `FIRST LETTERS IN KERALA.`

segments.voice: The tenth day after the nine nights is Vijayadashami, the victory tenth. In much of North India it's Dussehra, and it belongs to Rama: many towns stage the Ramlila for nine nights, and on the tenth, Ravana burns. In Bengal it's the last day of Durga Puja, when women smear sindoor on each other before the Goddess goes to the river. So why do Rama and Durga share a day? Bengal's own Ramayana, by the poet Krittivas, tells a story Valmiki doesn't. Before the last battle with Ravana, Rama worships the Goddess, out of season, in autumn. He needs a hundred and eight blue lotuses, and Hanuman brings them. But at the last offering, one lotus is missing: the Goddess has hidden it, to test him. Rama remembers that people call his eyes lotus-like. He lifts an arrow to offer one of his own eyes. And Durga appears, stops his hand, and blesses him with victory. Here's the teaching. In Hinduism the Goddess is Shakti, the power behind every victory, even a god's. Rama, Vishnu come down, still bows to her before he fights. So many families treat the victory tenth as the best day to begin. The day before, much of the South honors tools and books on Ayudha Puja; on the tenth, in Kerala, many small children write their first letters in rice, an elder guiding their finger. You start something with her blessing, because the strength to finish it is hers.
screen: `VIJAYADASHAMI: THE VICTORY TENTH.` · `WHY RAMA AND DURGA SHARE A DAY.` · `ONE MISSING. HE OFFERS HIS EYE.` · `SHAKTI: THE POWER BEHIND THE VICTORY.` · then, large: `EVEN RAMA BOWED TO THE GODDESS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Place in front of you, or picture, one tool you use every day: a pen, a phone, your own hands. Look at it the way people on Ayudha Puja do, with thanks. Then name one thing you're about to begin. If you pray, ask the Goddess, as Durga or Saraswati or simply Ma, for the strength to see it through. If you don't pray, take one slow breath before you start, the way Rama paused to bow before he fought.
Navaratri. Nine nights of the Goddess that end on Vijayadashami: Ravana burned in the North, Durga's farewell in Bengal, first letters in the South, and all of it her strength.
